fl-01.title: French and Its Alphabet
explain: **French** is one of the **Romance languages**, which descend from Latin. It belongs to the same family as Spanish and Italian. It is spoken not only in France but also in parts of Belgium and Switzerland, in Quebec in Canada, and in many countries in Africa. In this department we study both the French language and the writing produced in it. As a first step, we begin with the letters.

French uses the same 26 Roman letters as English. However, some letters carry an **accent mark** above or below them. The marks are not decoration but part of the spelling, so leaving one out gives a wrong spelling and sometimes a different word.

explain.alt: A table of French accent marks. It has five rows, and each row lists the symbol, its name, an example, and an approximate sound. é is accent aigu, example café, approx. ka-FEH. è is accent grave, example mère, approx. mehr. ê is accent circonflexe, example être, approx. ehtr. à is accent grave, example là, approx. la. ç is cédille, example garçon, approx. gar-SOHN.

explain:
- **é** (accent aigu): a closed 'eh' sound, with the mouth narrow.
- **è**, **ê** (accent grave, accent circonflexe): a more open 'eh' sound.
- **à**: the sound is the same as a; it serves to distinguish words.
- **ç** (cédille): normally c sounds like 'k' before a, o, u, but ç sounds like s.

English spelling would render é and è both as 'eh', but in reality the mouth opens to different degrees and they sound like different vowels. All the sound respellings in this lesson are only **approximations**; exact sounds cannot be captured in written letters. From now on, understand any respelling of a sound as an approximation of this kind.

examples.title: Pairs of words distinguished by one mark
body: *a* is a form of the verb avoir 'to have' (*il a*, he has), while *à* is a preposition meaning 'to, at, in' (*à Paris*, in Paris). They sound the same, but with or without the mark they are different words.
*la* is the article placed before a feminine noun, while *là* means 'there'. These two also sound the same and are distinguished by the mark.

examples.title: c and ç
body: The c in *café* comes before a, so it sounds like 'k', giving something close to 'ka-FEH'. The ç in *garçon* (boy, approx. gar-SOHN) also comes before a but sounds like s. So in the same position, c and ç make different sounds.

fl-02.title: Pronunciation and Silent Letters
explain: French is not read letter by letter as written. Letters that are written but not pronounced are called **silent letters**. There are rules linking spelling and sound, but you have to know the rules to read. This lesson covers the two things beginners meet first: silent letters and liaison. The sound respellings here are again all **approximations**.

**Consonants at the end of a word are mostly not pronounced.** This is true of the final t in *petit* (small, approx. puh-TEE), the d in *grand* (big, approx. GRAHN), and the s in *vous* (you, approx. voo). A final e is also silent. But when an e is added, the consonant before it is no longer at the end of the word, so it is pronounced. *petit* is close to puh-TEE and *petite* to puh-TEET; *grand* is close to GRAHN and *grande* to GRAHND.

explain.alt: A figure showing the silent letters of words. The first row is five letter boxes for petit; the last box, t, is dotted gray and labeled silent, and the word is read puh-TEE. The second row is six letter boxes for petite; the last box, e, is dotted gray and silent, the t is pronounced, and the word is read puh-TEET. The third row shows two words, vous and avez; the s box of vous and the a box of avez are outlined in orange and joined by a curve, and the pair is read voo za-VEH.

explain: This rule has many exceptions. Final c, r, f, and l are often pronounced (*sac* approx. sak, *bonjour* approx. bohn-ZHOOR, *neuf* approx. nuhf, *mal* approx. mal). So when you meet a new word, it is best to learn its sound along with it. Also, h is not pronounced, so *hôtel* (hotel) is read as if it began with a vowel, close to oh-TEL.

**Liaison** is the phenomenon in which, when the next word begins with a vowel, a consonant at the end of the preceding word that is normally silent is linked to the following word and pronounced. *vous avez* (you have) is close to voo za-VEH, and *les amis* (the friends) is close to lay za-MEE. Here the s takes on a sound close to z. Where liaison occurs is fixed by grammar, so it does not happen in every case. For now, it is enough to know the concept.

Let us also note why the respellings are only approximations. The French r sound, the nasal vowels made through the nose (*bon*, close to bohn with a nasal vowel), and the rounded-lip vowels have no exact match in English letters. To learn the sounds accurately you must hear them, and since this classroom does not play audio, the aim here is to get a feel for the rules.

fl-03.title: Noun Gender and Articles
explain: Every French noun belongs to one of two classes, **masculine** or **feminine**. This is called **gender** (grammatical gender). People and animals mostly follow their actual sex (*le père* the father, *la mère* the mother). But objects also have gender. *le livre* (book) is masculine and *la table* (table) is feminine. The gender of an object cannot be known from its meaning, so it is best to memorize words together with their articles. Korean has neither gender nor articles, so this feels unfamiliar at first.

An **article** is a small word placed before a noun. To refer to a specific, identified thing, we use the **definite article** (le, la, les); to refer to one or several unidentified things, we use the **indefinite article** (un, une, des). Articles change according to the gender and number of the noun.

explain.alt: A table of French articles. The columns are masculine singular, feminine singular, and plural. The definite article row is le livre, la table, les livres, and the indefinite article row is un livre, une table, des livres. Below is a note that before a vowel le and la are reduced to l', with the examples l'école (school, feminine) and l'ami (friend, masculine).

explain: In approximate English respelling, le is close to luh, la to lah, les to lay, un to uhn (a nasal vowel), and des to day. The plural is mostly formed by adding s to the noun, and this s is silent. So *livre* and *livres* sound the same, and in speech singular and plural are told apart by the difference between le and les.

There are also tendencies that help you guess gender. For example, nouns ending in *-tion* (*la nation*) are mostly feminine, and nouns ending in *-ment* (*le moment*) are mostly masculine. But these are only tendencies and have exceptions, so the habit of writing the article together with each word is the most reliable way to memorize.

examples.title: Words whose form changes with gender
body: *un étudiant* is a male student and *une étudiante* is a female student. The feminine form adds e, so the preceding consonant is pronounced. This is the same relationship as petit and petite in the previous lesson.
People of different sexes, like *le garçon* (boy) and *la fille* (girl), are often entirely different words.

fl-04.title: être, avoir, and -er Verbs
explain: French verbs change their form according to the subject. This is called **conjugation**. First let us learn the **personal pronouns** used as subjects: *je* (I), *tu* (you), *il* (he), *elle* (she), *nous* (we), *vous* (you, plural or formal), *ils* (they, masculine or mixed), *elles* (they, feminine). *tu* is used among close acquaintances, and *vous* is used when speaking to several people or when speaking politely. *je* is reduced to *j'* before a vowel.
The two most important verbs are **être** (to be) and **avoir** (to have). They are irregular and must be memorized as they are.

explain.alt: A verb conjugation table. The columns are être (to be), avoir (to have), and parler (to speak), and the rows are I, you, he/she, we, you (plural/formal), and they. être: je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont. avoir: j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont. parler: je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent. A note below says that elle uses the same form as il, and elles the same form as ils.

explain: The third column, **parler** (to speak), is the model **-er verb**. Most verbs whose infinitive ends in -er follow the same rule: to the stem *parl-* we add *-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent*. *habiter* (to live) and *chanter* (to sing) work the same way. There are a few exceptions, but this rule is the most common.

There is a point to note about sound. The endings of *je parle*, *tu parles*, *il parle*, and *ils parlent* are all silent, so they all sound the same, close to the approximation 'parl'. Even though the spellings differ, they cannot be told apart in speech. By contrast, *nous parlons* (approx. par-LOHN) and *vous parlez* (approx. par-LAY) sound different.

examples.title: Making short sentences
body: *Je suis étudiant.* I am a (male) student. / *Elle est étudiante.* She is a student.
*Nous avons un chat.* We have a cat. / *Ils parlent français.* They speak French.
From the form of the verb in a sentence you can guess who the subject is. Even so, French does not drop the subject and always writes it.

fl-05.title: Basic Expressions: Greetings and Numbers 0 to 10
explain:
In this lesson we learn expressions you can use right away when meeting people. Remember that all the sound respellings are **approximations**.
- *Bonjour.* Hello. (approx. bohn-ZHOOR) A greeting for daytime.
- *Bonsoir.* An evening greeting. (approx. bohn-SWAR)
- *Salut.* A casual greeting among close acquaintances, used both on meeting and on parting. (approx. sa-LU)
- *Au revoir.* Goodbye. (approx. oh ruh-VWAR)
- *Merci.* Thank you. (approx. mehr-SEE)
- *S'il vous plaît.* Please. (approx. seel voo PLEH)
- *Oui. / Non.* Yes. / No.
- *Excusez-moi.* Excuse me.

Expressions for asking how someone is differ in formality. *Comment allez-vous ?* politely asks how someone is doing, while *Ça va ?* is a casual question closer to 'How's it going?' A reply is something like *Ça va bien, merci.* (I'm well, thank you). A name is given as in *Je m'appelle Marc.* (My name is Marc), and a polite way to ask a name is *Comment vous appelez-vous ?*

examples.title: A short first-meeting conversation
body:
- *Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Marc. Et vous ?* Hello! My name is Marc. And you?
- *Je m'appelle Léa. Enchantée.* My name is Léa. Pleased to meet you.
*Enchanté* is used by a man and *Enchantée* by a woman. It is the same principle as adding an e according to gender, which we saw earlier. *Et* means 'and' and is read close to 'eh'.

fl-06.title: Reading Short Texts and Writing a Self-Introduction
explain: Let us gather what we have learned so far and read a short text. The text below is a fictional one made for this classroom. When reading, do not stop at unknown words; it is better to look first for frames you already know. If you see verbs learned earlier, such as *Je suis*, *J'ai*, and *je parle*, the skeleton of the sentence takes shape.

explain.alt: A short text of eight numbered sentences, with the English meaning under each sentence. 1 Bonjour! Hello. 2 Je m'appelle Léa. My name is Léa. 3 Je suis étudiante. I am a student (female). 4 J'habite à Lyon. I live in Lyon. 5 J'ai un chat. I have a cat. 6 Le chat est petit. The cat is small. 7 Je parle français et coréen. I speak French and Korean. 8 Au revoir! Goodbye.

explain: Let us go over the new words. *habiter* is an -er verb meaning 'to live', so it gives *j'habite* (I live). The h is silent, so je is reduced to j'. *à* means 'to, at, in', so *à Lyon* is 'in Lyon'. *et* is 'and' and *petit* is 'small'. *étudiante* is a female student, and for a male student it is *étudiant*.

fl-07.title: The Aspectual Contrast of French Past Tenses: Passé Composé, Imparfait, and Plus-que-parfait
explain: Korean expresses most past events with a single pre-final ending, '-eoss/ass-', but French strictly distinguishes the **passé composé** and the **imparfait** according to **aspect**, the viewpoint from which the past is seen. The difference between these two tenses is not a difference in the absolute time at which an event occurred, but whether the speaker sees the event as **a point that has been closed off (perfective aspect)** or as **a line that continues without boundaries (imperfective aspect)**.

The **passé composé** is formed by combining the present tense of the auxiliary *avoir* (or *être* in the case of verbs of motion and coming and going and of pronominal verbs) with the **past participle**. It expresses a one-time event with a clear beginning and end, an instantaneous change, or a repetition with a fixed number of times (*trois fois*, three times), and in narrative texts it takes the role of the **foreground** (Premier plan), which moves the plot forward. The **imparfait**, by contrast, is formed by adding the imperfect endings (*-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*) to the stem of the first person plural (*nous*) of the present indicative, and it expresses states that were in progress in the past, descriptions of the setting, and habitual repetition, taking the role of the **background** (Arrière-plan).

explain.alt: A timeline and comparison table of French past tenses. The imparfait is shown as a continuous background line, the passé composé as a point for a completed event, and the plus-que-parfait as a point earlier still; the table at the bottom summarizes form, aspectual feature, and narrative role.
explain.caption: When the imparfait unfolds the curtain of the background, the passé composé stages the event on top of it.

explain: A typical construction in which the two tenses meet in one sentence is *Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti* (It was raining when I went out). The rain falling (*Il pleuvait*, imparfait) is a background that began before I went out and continued after, while my opening the door and going out (*je suis sorti*, passé composé) is a completed event that broke through the middle of that background. To express an **event completed one step earlier** than the reference event in the past, we use the **plus-que-parfait** (*avait/était + past participle*), in which the auxiliary is put in the imparfait.

The trickiest grammatical rule in using the passé composé and plus-que-parfait is **agreement of the past participle** (Accord du participe passé) in gender and number. With verbs that take the auxiliary **être**, the past participle always agrees in gender and number with the **subject** (*Elle est partie*). With verbs that take the auxiliary **avoir**, the participle does not agree when the object comes after the verb, but when the **direct object (COD) is placed before the verb** (the pronouns *le, la, les*, the relative pronoun *que*, and so on), the past participle must agree in gender and number with that **preceding direct object**. For example, in *les lettres que j'ai écrites* (the letters I wrote), the feminine plural ending *-es* is added to *écrites* precisely because the relative pronoun *que*, which stands for the antecedent *les lettres* (feminine plural), is placed before the verb.

examples.title: Distributing the imparfait, passé composé, and plus-que-parfait in a narrative context
body: Condition: "The night was dark (1). She was walking through the garden (2). Suddenly someone called her name (3). She had thought he had already left (4)."
Step 1: (1) and (2) are the scenery and an action in progress before the event occurs (background), so we use the **imparfait** (*La nuit était sombre. Elle marchait...*).

Step 2: (3) is an instantaneous event that broke the background, so we use the **passé composé** (*quelqu'un a appelé...*), and in (4) his having left is further back in the past than the moment of calling, so we use the **plus-que-parfait** (*il était déjà parti*).
Interpretation: the combination of these three past tenses alone lets a French sentence create a three-dimensional perspective of time.

Step 1: In sentence A, the feminine plural direct object *ces fleurs* comes after the verb, so the past participle *acheté* does not change.

Step 2: In sentence B, the direct object pronoun *les* (= *ces fleurs*, feminine plural) comes before the auxiliary *ai*, so the feminine plural ending *-es* is added to the past participle, which is written *achetées*.
Interpretation: both are pronounced alike, approx. [ah-shuh-TAY], but they are strictly distinguished in spelling.

fl-08.title: Syntax and Pragmatics of the Subjunctive: Volition, Emotion, Doubt, and Concession
explain: The French **subjunctive** (Subjonctif) is used mainly in subordinate clauses introduced by the conjunction **que**; it is a mood that does not assert an event as objective fact but presents it inflected through the speaker's **subjective attitude (volition, emotion, doubt, judgment)**. Conversely, when the main-clause verb conveys a fact objectively or declares certainty (*Je sais que...*, *Il est certain que...*), the **indicative** (Indicatif) is used.

The present subjunctive is formed by adding *-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent* to the stem of the third person plural (*ils*) of the present indicative (however, core verbs such as *être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir, vouloir* have irregular stems). The syntactic environments that obligatorily call for the subjunctive fall into four broad categories. First, **volition, command, wish, and demand** (*vouloir que, demander que, souhaiter que*). Second, **emotion, regret, joy, and fear** (*être heureux que, regretter que, craindre que*). Third, **necessity, obligation, and subjective value judgment** (*il faut que, il est important que, il est dommage que*). Fourth, **doubt, negation, and uncertainty** (*douter que, nier que, il est possible que*).

Of special note is the alternation of mood according to the polarity (affirmative/negative) of **verbs of thinking and opinion** (*penser, croire, trouver*) and of **expressions of certainty**. In the affirmative sentences *Je pense qu'il **vient*** (I think he is coming) and *Il est sûr qu'il **vient*** (It is certain that he is coming), the speaker believes the fact to be true, so the **indicative** is used. But if these are turned into a negative sentence or an inverted question and the conviction wavers, as in *Je ne pense pas qu'il **vienne*** (I don't think he is coming), the subordinate verb changes to the **subjunctive**.

Among conjunctions of adverbial clauses too, the mood divides according to meaning. After *parce que* and *puisque*, which express cause, the indicative follows because the cause is a fact that has already occurred, but after conjunctions of purpose (*pour que, afin que*, in order that), concession (*bien que, quoique*, although), temporal precedence (*avant que*, before), and negative condition (*sans que*, without) the subjunctive always follows.

Furthermore, when the subject of the main clause and the subject of the subordinate clause are the same, French, following its principle of economy, does not use a *que + subjunctive* clause but must contract it into an **infinitive construction** (Infinitif). For example, "I want to leave" is not written \**Je veux que je parte* (ungrammatical) but **Je veux partir**, and in place of the conjunction *avant que* (when the subjects differ) one uses the preposition *avant de + infinitive* (when the subject is the same).

body: Condition: change the main clause of sentence A *Il est certain qu'elle **sait** la vérité* (It is certain that she knows the truth) into the negative *Il n'est pas certain...*.
Step 1: The affirmative main clause *Il est certain* expresses 100% certainty, so it takes the indicative *sait*.

Step 2: The negative main clause *Il n'est pas certain* (It is not certain) moves into the realm of uncertainty and doubt, so the subordinate verb *savoir* must be changed into the present subjunctive **sache**.
Interpretation: *Il n'est pas certain qu'elle sache la vérité.* (The change of mood directly reflects the speaker's degree of epistemic certainty.)

fl-09.title: The Conditional, the Si-Clause System, and Pronoun Word Order
explain: The French **conditional** (Conditionnel) is formed by combining the simple future stem (the form ending in *-r*) with the imperfect endings (*-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*). This morphological combination itself shows the two essential natures of the conditional. The first is the **future seen from a past point in time** (Futur dans le passé, e.g. *Il a dit qu'il **viendrait***, He said that he would come), and the second is the **hypothetical, unreal, and softened register** that is tied to a condition.

**Si (if) conditional sentences** follow three levels of strict tense-correlation formulas according to how likely the condition is to be realized. (1) **A realizable present or future condition**: `Si + present indicative, main clause in the present indicative/simple future` (*S'il fait beau demain, nous sortirons*). (2) **An unreal supposition contrary to present fact**, or a future supposition with little chance of realization: `Si + imperfect indicative, main clause in the present conditional` (*Si j'avais le temps maintenant, je voyagerais*). (3) **An unreal supposition contrary to a past fact that has already passed**: `Si + pluperfect indicative, main clause in the past conditional` (*Si tu m'avais appelé hier, je serais venu*). The most important grammatical constraint here is the rule that **immediately after the conditional si, the simple future or a conditional form (an *-r-* stem) can never appear**.

The conditional is also actively used on its own outside conditional sentences. Typical cases are the **conditional of softening tone**, which gently eases a request (*Je voudrais un café*, *Pourriez-vous m'aider?*), and the **journalistic conditional**, which relays news not yet confirmed in media reports without asserting it (*Selon la police, le suspect **serait** à l'étranger*, According to the police, the suspect is reportedly abroad).

Another key to deciphering French sentences is the **word order, before the verb, of double object pronouns and the neuter pronouns (y, en)**. When two pronouns stand together before the verb in affirmative, negative, and interrogative sentences, they strictly follow this five-column order: **column 1** (*me, te, se, nous, vous*) → **column 2** (third-person direct object *le, la, les*) → **column 3** (third-person indirect object *lui, leur*) → **column 4** (place and the preposition *à* + the thing pronoun *y*) → **column 5** (the preposition *de* + the thing and partitive pronoun *en*).

For example, in *Il donne le livre à Marie* (He gives the book to Marie), if *le livre* is replaced by *le* (column 2) and *à Marie* by *lui* (column 3), we get **Il le lui donne**. In *Il me donne le livre* (He gives me the book), by contrast, *me* (column 1) comes before *le* (column 2), so we get **Il me le donne**. In the passé composé, this whole pronoun cluster is placed before the auxiliary (*Il me l'a donné*).

examples.title: Assembling a si-clause contrary to a past fact
body: Condition: the fact is *Je n'ai pas su ton adresse, donc je ne t'ai pas écrit.* (I did not know your address, and so I did not write to you.)
Step 1: Because it is contrary to a past fact, the *si* clause takes the **pluperfect** (*avais su*) and the main clause takes the **past conditional** (*aurais écrit*).
Step 2: *si* contracts to *s'il* before the vowel *i*, but it does not contract before *je* and becomes *si j'avais*.
Interpretation: *Si j'avais su ton adresse, je t'aurais écrit.* (If I had known your address, I would have written to you.)

examples.title: Practicing double-pronoun arrangement before the verb
body: Condition: replace the nouns with pronouns in the sentences *Paul prête sa voiture à ses amis* (Paul lends his car to his friends) and *Elle parle de ce projet au directeur* (She talks about this project to the director).
Step 1: In the first sentence, *sa voiture* becomes *la* (column 2) and *à ses amis* becomes *leur* (column 3), so following the order column 2 → column 3 gives **Paul la leur prête**.

Step 2: In the second sentence, *de ce projet* is a thing, so it becomes *en* (column 5), and *au directeur* is a person, so it becomes *lui* (column 3); following the order column 3 → column 5 gives **Elle lui en parle**.
Interpretation: the first and second persons (*me, te, nous, vous*) come before *le/la/les*, but the third-person indirect pronouns (*lui, leur*) and *y, en* always come after *le/la/les*.

fl-10.title: 17th-Century French Classical Tragedy: The Three Unities, Corneille, and Racine
explain: Seventeenth-century France was the **Grand Siècle** (Great Century), which held supremacy over European culture against the background of the establishment of Louis XIV's absolute monarchy and the rationalist philosophy of Descartes. The aesthetics of **Classicism** (Classicisme) that took shape in this period sought to rein in the disorderly and exaggerated imagination of the Renaissance and Baroque eras and to explore a universal human nature transcending time and place through **reason (Raison), order, balance, and restraint**. The poet Boileau declared in his *Art poétique* (*L'Art poétique*, 1674): "Love reason; let your writings always draw their light and value from reason alone."

The three pillars governing classical drama were the **rule of the three unities** (Règle des trois unités), **verisimilitude** (Vraisemblance), and **propriety** (Bienséance). First, the rule of the three unities holds that "only a single event, completed within one day and in one place, should be put on stage." That is, **unity of action**, excluding subplots; **unity of time**, in which the time of the play does not exceed 24 hours; and **unity of place**, in which the stage is fixed as a single room or square. Second, verisimilitude is the principle that even an extraordinary event that really happened in history cannot be staged unless it can be plausibly accepted by the spectator's reason. Third, under the norm of propriety (decorum), directly showing bloody murder, duels, and physical violence on stage was strictly forbidden, so tragic catastrophes were conveyed only through a messenger's **narrative speech** (Récit).

explain.alt: A diagram comparing the norms of 17th-century classical drama (the rule of the three unities, verisimilitude and propriety, Corneille, Racine, Molière) with 18th-century Enlightenment literature (the Encyclopédie, Montesquieu, Voltaire, Rousseau, Beaumarchais).
explain.caption: From the strict verse form and exploration of human nature of the 17th century, literature moves in the 18th century toward prose and satire for the critique of social institutions.

explain: Classical tragedy was written in **alexandrine** (Alexandrin) verse, the rhymed twelve-syllable line, and two great masters, **Pierre Corneille** (1606-1684) and **Jean Racine** (1639-1699), formed a matched pair. In the terms of the writers La Rochefoucauld and La Bruyère, **Corneille portrayed "how man ought to be," and Racine portrayed "how man actually is."**

In Corneille's masterpiece **Le Cid** (1637), the young nobleman Rodrigue agonizes between the **honor and duty** (Devoir) of his family, which requires him to kill his beloved Chimène's father in a duel, and his **love** (Amour) for her, but through a strong will he fulfills his duty and stands out as a hero. By contrast, in Racine's masterpiece **Phèdre** (1677), influenced by the pessimistic view of man of Jansenism, the heroine Phèdre, though better than anyone aware through reason that her forbidden passion (Passion) for her stepson Hippolyte is a sin, cannot overcome her own feelings and plunges into the abyss of jealousy and ruin.

examples.title: Comparing the tragic conflicts of Corneille's Le Cid and Racine's Phèdre
body: Condition: Corneille's protagonist Rodrigue and Racine's protagonist Phèdre both experience a clash between moral duty and personal feeling.
Step 1: Rodrigue controls his feelings with reason and free will, chooses the duty owed to family and state, and achieves moral sublimity (heroism).
Step 2: Phèdre, though clearly conscious through reason of her own guilt, is seized by a dark fate and destructive passion and cannot save herself.
Interpretation: if Corneille showed the triumph of the will (a tragedy of voluntarism), Racine perfected the fate of man helpless before passion (a pure tragedy of passion).

body: Condition: in the last act of Racine's Phèdre, the innocent young man Hippolyte is dragged off by a monster on the seashore and dies a gruesome death.
Step 1: Under the norm of propriety (Bienséance) of 17th-century classicism, a monster or a bleeding corpse cannot be brought directly onto the stage.
Step 2: Instead, the tutor Théramène appears on stage and vividly describes Hippolyte's end in finely wrought twelve-syllable alexandrine verse ("Théramène's narrative").
Interpretation: the constraint of excluding visual shock instead had the effect of maximizing the poetic density of the language and the inner psychological terror.

fl-11.title: Molière's Classical Comedy and the 17th-Century Moralists (Pascal and La Rochefoucauld)
explain: If Corneille and Racine set up the summit of classical tragedy, **Molière** (real name Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, 1622-1673) sharply dissected the false consciousness of French society of his day and the flaws of human character, raising the **comedy of character** (Comédie de caractère) to a rank of art no lower than tragedy. The principle his comedies upheld was the maxim of the ancient poet Horace, **"to correct manners by laughter"** (*Castigat ridendo mores*).

The protagonists of Molière's comedies are mostly people who, seized by a single obsession or defect, have lost their sense of rational balance (**the golden mean**, Juste milieu). **Tartuffe** satirizes the religious hypocrite Tartuffe, who poses as a devout believer and tries to swallow up the entire household of the wealthy bourgeois Orgon, and Orgon, who has fallen into blind fanaticism, and it suffered fierce suppression from the religious circles of the day. In **L'Avare**, Harpagon, because of his paranoia about money, would even trade his children's happiness for a box of gold coins, and in **Le Bourgeois gentilhomme**, Monsieur Jourdain, blinded by his aping of the nobility, is made a plaything by swindlers.

One of his greatest masterpieces, **Le Misanthrope** (1666), goes beyond simple poetic justice and shows a deep philosophical ambivalence. The protagonist Alceste hates the flattery and hypocrisy of high society and demands only 'absolute honesty' at all times and in all places, but his uncompromising fastidiousness turns out to be yet another extreme that makes coexistence in human society impossible. His friend Philinte, by contrast, represents the attitude of the classical cultivated gentleman (**honnête homme**, Honnête homme), who accepts human flaws as they are and lives by amiable reason.

The 17th-century thinkers who coolly observed human nature and social customs in this way and recorded them in short reflections or maxims are called, in the history of French literature, the **moralists** (Moralistes). Here morale (Morale) means not simple moral preaching but **anthropological reflection on human psychology, customs, and character (Mœurs)**.

The representative moralist **La Rochefoucauld**, in his *Maximes* (*Maximes*, 1665), declared that "our virtues are most often but vices in disguise," and ruthlessly dissected the **self-love** (Amour-propre, selfishness) lurking at the bottom of every noble act that seems altruistic. Meanwhile **Blaise Pascal**, mathematician and philosopher, in his posthumous collection **Pensées** (Pensées, 1670), faced squarely the weakness and wretchedness of man caught between the infinitely vast universe and the infinitely small microscopic world, yet through the proposition **"Man is but a reed, but a thinking reed"** he stressed the dignity of thought and the leap to faith.

examples.title: The structure of hypocrisy exposed in Molière's Tartuffe
body: Condition: the head of the household, Orgon, deceived by the false piety of the hypocrite Tartuffe, forces his daughter into marriage and even hands over the deed giving away his entire fortune, but his wife Elmire hides Orgon under the table and has him witness with his own eyes Tartuffe's true colors as a seducer.
Step 1: Blind faith (fanaticism), which would not wake however much it was argued with in words, is shattered only through sensory evidence before his eyes.
Step 2: By distinguishing true faith from outward hypocrisy, Molière avoided the accusation of attacking religion itself and aimed squarely at the hypocritical customs of his day.
Interpretation: it shows the power of classical comedy to dismantle authority and blind belief through the weapon of laughter.

examples.title: A comparative reading of La Rochefoucauld's Maximes and Pascal's Pensées
body: Condition: La Rochefoucauld wrote, "The pity we often feel at the misfortunes of others is only a foreboding of misfortunes that may befall us," and Pascal wrote, "Even a king, if left to sit alone in a room with no amusement (diversion, Divertissement) and made to think about himself, immediately becomes unhappy."
Step 1: Both thinkers sharply see through how cleverly human beings deceive themselves (self-deception).

Step 2: La Rochefoucauld exposed the mechanism of selfishness (self-love) through concise paradoxes within salon culture, while Pascal revealed the existential wretchedness of people clinging to 'diversions' such as hunting, gambling, and power to forget death and emptiness, and so turned them toward God.
Interpretation: the psychological dissection of the 17th-century moralists later became the deep root of the French tradition of the psychological novel.

fl-12.title: 18th-Century Enlightenment (Lumières) Literature: The Encyclopedists, Montesquieu, Voltaire, and Rousseau
explain: The 18th century, running from the death of the Sun King Louis XIV in 1715 to the French Revolution of 1789, was the **Age of Enlightenment** (Siècle des Lumières), which sought through the light of reason (*Lumières*) to break down ignorance and superstition and the dogmatism of absolute monarchy and the Church. Where 17th-century classicism explored universal human psychology within the system, the 18th-century Enlightenment philosophers and writers (*Philosophes*) made literature a **practical weapon for reforming the inequality and religious fanaticism of the Ancien Régime**.

The central tower of this great intellectual movement was the **Encyclopédie** (1751-1772, 28 volumes in all), completed over some twenty years by Denis **Diderot** and the mathematician **d'Alembert**. The Encyclopédie dismantled the theology-centered medieval system of knowledge and, drawing on human memory (history), reason (philosophy and science), and imagination (the arts), compiled all the learning and craft techniques of the day, spreading critical enlightenment to the bourgeois class.

To criticize society while evading censorship, writers developed ingenious prose forms. In **Lettres persanes** (1721), **Montesquieu** borrowed the epistolary form of letters sent home by two Persian travelers visiting Paris (Usbek and Rica) and, through the unfamiliar eyes of foreigners, scathingly satirized the French absolute monarchy and the authority of the pope. Later, in *De l'esprit des lois* (1748), he established the theory of the **separation of powers** among the legislative, judicial, and executive branches.

**Voltaire** (1694-1778), the symbol of the Enlightenment, fought all his life against religious intolerance and fanaticism, and perfected a new genre, the short and witty **philosophical tale** (Conte philosophique). His masterpiece **Candide, ou l'Optimisme** (1759) tells how the naive young Candide, a believer in Leibniz's philosophy ("this is the best of all possible worlds"), experiences with his whole body the horrors of war, the Lisbon earthquake, the Inquisition, and slavery, and comes to realize the illusion of metaphysical optimism. The novel ends with the famous line that calls on us to stop empty argument and earnestly build our lives in reality, **"We must cultivate our garden"** (*Il faut cultiver notre jardin*).

**Jean-Jacques Rousseau** (1712-1778), by contrast, cast fundamental doubt, from the very midst of the Enlightenment, on optimism about reason and the progress of civilization. Criticizing the good man in the state of nature as corrupted by civilization and the institution of private property, he established in **Du contrat social** the principles of popular sovereignty and the general will (Volonté générale). At the same time, by deeply revealing solitary walks in nature, intimate sensibility, and subjective sincerity in the epistolary novel *Julie, ou la Nouvelle Héloïse* and in **Les Confessions**, the forerunner of the modern autobiography, he became a **precursor of the Romanticism of the coming 19th century**.

examples.title: The satirical technique of the 'unfamiliar gaze' in Montesquieu's Lettres persanes
body: Condition: the Persian Rica, seeing the king (Louis XIV) and the pope in Paris, writes in a letter: "The King of France is a magician who rules even the minds of his subjects. If he needs a million crowns, he mints half a million, and if he orders them to believe that this is a million crowns, everyone believes it. A greater magician is the pope, who makes them believe that three is only one (the Trinity)."
Step 1: The currency debasement policy and the Catholic doctrine, taken for granted by the French, are described as 'bizarre magic' through the eyes of a Muslim traveler.
Step 2: In an age when direct criticism brought immediate banning of books and imprisonment, the naive astonishment of a foreigner is used as a mask to get around censorship.
Interpretation: it is the essence of Enlightenment satirical literature, dismantling the absoluteness of one's own culture through a relativist gaze.

examples.title: Interpreting the 'cultivating the garden' ending of Voltaire's Candide
body: Condition: the tutor Pangloss, even after suffering every kind of disaster, insists to the end that "everything is connected for the best." To this Candide answers, "That is well said, but now we must cultivate our garden."
Step 1: Neither the metaphysical speculation that rationalizes the evils of the world (Pangloss's optimism) nor the pessimism that gives up on the world solves the problem.
Step 2: 'Cultivating the garden' means leaving behind grand empty theorizing and working in sweat and solidarity in the concrete realm of reality that human beings can change by their own power.
Interpretation: it is the conclusion of Voltaire's Enlightenment thought, which stressed practical reason and a civic work ethic.

fl-13.title: From 19th-Century Romanticism to Realism (Stendhal and Balzac)
explain: In the first half of the 19th century, when the Restoration monarchy was installed after the French Revolution and the fall of the Napoleonic Empire, the movement that voiced the disillusionment and passion of the young generation was **French Romanticism** (Romantisme). Ever since Chateaubriand, in *René*, gave voice to the **malady of the century** (Mal du siècle), the aimless melancholy and solitude of modern youth, the poets Lamartine and Musset sang in lyric poetry of lost time and the anguish of love.

The commander-in-chief of French Romanticism was the poet, dramatist, and novelist **Victor Hugo** (1802-1885). In the preface to his play *Cromwell* (1827), he broke down classicism's rule of the three unities and its division of genres, declaring that the whole truth of life can be captured only when the sublime (Sublime) and the ugly and grotesque (Grotesque) are mixed on one stage. The fierce clash staged in the theater on the opening night of his play **Hernani** in 1830 between the defenders of classicism and the young Romantics (the **Battle of Hernani**) was the signal that announced the victory of Romanticism. Through *Notre-Dame de Paris* and the epic novel **Les Misérables** (1862), Hugo later combined romantic passion with a humanitarian vision of social justice.

But after the July Revolution of 1830, when a capitalist society ruled by the financial bourgeoisie took full shape, the **Realist** (Réalisme) novel emerged, which in place of romantic heroic tales coolly analyzed how **money, desire, social climbing, and social environment** move human beings. Its forerunners were **Stendhal** (real name Henri Beyle, 1783-1842) and **Honoré de Balzac** (1799-1850).

In **Le Rouge et le Noir** (1830), Stendhal portrayed the ambition and ruin of Julien Sorel, the son of a commoner carpenter, who in the Restoration era, when the Napoleonic-era uniform (**red**, Rouge) had vanished, chooses the black cassock (**black**, Noir) of the clergy to rise in station. Stendhal compared the novel to **"a mirror carried along the high road,"** and with a style as dry and lucid and free of padding as the Napoleonic Code, he keenly captured the characters' inner psychology and the feelings of love (crystallization, Cristallisation).

**Balzac**, by contrast, through the enormous series **La Comédie humaine** (La Comédie humaine), which binds together some ninety novels, sought to become the 'secretary of the history of manners' of the whole of 19th-century French society. Just as the zoologist Buffon classified animal species according to their natural environment, he created a variety of **human types** that change with social environment, occupation, and wealth (Father Goriot's blind paternal love, Père Grandet's miserliness, Rastignac's ambition to get ahead). In particular, he established Balzacian realism through the **technique of reappearing characters**, in which a supporting character in one novel reappears as a lead in another, and through the minute description, over dozens of pages, of the wallpaper, furniture, and dress of the boardinghouse where a character lives, showing that environment is itself the character's nature.

examples.title: Reading the title symbolism and the 'mirror' metaphor of Stendhal's Le Rouge et le Noir
body: Condition: Stendhal wrote in Le Rouge et le Noir, "A novel is a mirror carried along a high road. At one moment it reflects the blue of the sky, at another the mud of the puddles on the road. And would you accuse the mirror of being immoral because it reflects the mud?"
Step 1: The norm of propriety of 17th-century classicism and moralizing critics attacked the novel for portraying hypocrisy and ambition (the mud) as immoral.

Step 2: Through the mirror metaphor, Stendhal defended the view that the novelist's task is not to beautify reality but to reflect, just as it is, both the ugliness and the beauty of the society of his day (the road).
Interpretation: this is the passage that most clearly declares the principle of objective representation in realist literature.

examples.title: The spatial description of the Maison Vauquer boardinghouse in Balzac's Le Père Goriot
body: Condition: in the opening of Le Père Goriot, Balzac minutely describes the shabby exterior of Madame Vauquer's boardinghouse on the edge of Paris, its musty dining room, its faded wallpaper, and the worn slippers of the proprietress. And he adds, "Just as her whole person explains the boardinghouse, the whole boardinghouse hints at her person."
Step 1: For Balzac, the description of space and objects is not mere background decoration but the material foundation that determines a character's class and nature.

Step 2: The positions of the boarders, arranged vertically from the ground floor to the attic according to the price of their rooms, are a scale model of the class pyramid of Parisian capitalist society.
Interpretation: the disillusionment that the provincial law student Rastignac experiences as he climbs from this bottom to high society runs through the whole of La Comédie humaine.

fl-14.title: Flaubert's Objective Description (Free Indirect Discourse) and Zola's Theory of the Naturalist Experimental Novel
explain: In Balzac's realism, an omniscient author still showed his face and commented on the characters' actions in moral and philosophical terms. The figure who thoroughly erased this subjective intervention and brought about a revolution in the style of the modern novel was **Gustave Flaubert** (1821-1880). He established the principle of **non-intervening objectivity** (Impassibilité, impassivity and impersonality), that "the artist in his work must be like God in the universe, present everywhere and visible nowhere," and he practiced the **doctrine of the mot juste** (Le mot juste), rewriting a sentence dozens of times to find the single exact noun and verb.

Flaubert's masterpiece **Madame Bovary** (1857) portrayed how Emma Bovary, the wife of a provincial doctor who dreamed of glittering aristocratic romance while reading popular love stories, ends her life by taking arsenic after tedious daily life, adultery, and a mountain of debt she cannot bear. Handling trite and ordinary material, he built a prose rhythm as perfect as poetry, showing the modern novel's ideal of "a book about nothing, held up by style alone."

explain.alt: A diagram comparing three movements of 19th-century French literature (Realism, Naturalism, Symbolism) by heyday, core, technique, aesthetics/themes, and representative writers.
explain.caption: In prose, Realism and Naturalism pushed objectivity and scientific experiment, while in poetry Symbolism pioneered the correspondence of the senses and suggestion.

explain: The most refined narrative technique Flaubert perfected is **free indirect discourse** (Style indirect libre). It is a technique that neither transcribes a character's words directly in quotation marks (direct discourse) nor binds them in a subordinate clause (a *que* clause) such as "she thought that..." (indirect discourse), but **melts the character's inner voice, with its exclamations and questions, directly into the imperfect (Imparfait) sentences of a third-person narrator**. Thanks to this, the narrator can ironically reveal the character's vanity and delusions without passing judgment directly.

From the late 1860s on, **Émile Zola** (1840-1902) combined realism with the experimental medicine method of the contemporary physiologist Claude Bernard to found **Naturalism** (Naturalisme). In his essay **Le Roman expérimental** (1880), Zola argued that the novelist should not remain a mere observer but should become an **experimenter** who proves what inevitable catastrophe occurs when a character with a particular **hereditary temperament (Hérédité)** is placed in a particular **social environment (Milieu)**.

Zola wrote the twenty-volume epic series **Les Rougon-Macquart** (Les Rougon-Macquart), tracing across five generations the hereditary madness, alcoholism, and social upheaval of one family under the Second Empire. Among them, *L'Assommoir*, portraying the downfall of Gervaise, a laundress among the Parisian lower classes, and **Germinal** (1885), portraying on a grand scale the wretched lives and strike struggle of the miners of the north, are ranked as the pinnacle of Naturalist literature. In 1898, to clear the name of the Jewish officer Dreyfus, Zola also published in the newspaper an open letter to the President, **"J'accuse...!"** (*J'accuse...!*), becoming the emblem of the engaged intellectual.

examples.title: Analyzing the free indirect discourse (Style indirect libre) in Flaubert's Madame Bovary
body: Condition: in the scene just after Emma falls into her first adultery, as she looks in the mirror and rejoices, the following sentences appear. *Elle allait donc posséder enfin ces joies de l'amour, cette fièvre du bonheur dont elle avait désespéré! Elle entrait dans quelque chose de merveilleux...* (So she was at last about to possess those joys of love, that fever of happiness of which she had despaired! She was entering into something marvelous...)
Step 1: The grammatical form consists of a third-person pronoun (*Elle*) and the imperfect (*allait, entrait*), so on the surface it looks like a sentence of the narrator.

Step 2: But the exclamation mark (!) and the trite, excited vocabulary such as 'something marvelous' and 'fever of happiness' are not the thoughts of the cool-headed author Flaubert but Emma's own deluded inner feelings.
Interpretation: by overlaying the narrator's sentence and the character's inner monologue without quotation marks or *Elle pensait que*, it ironically exposes the fleetingness of romantic illusion.

examples.title: The hereditary and environmental determinism and social indictment of Zola's Germinal
body: Condition: the young Étienne Lantier, who has inherited the genes of a family of alcoholics, takes a job in the Montsou mine in the north and leads a workers' strike amid the extreme conditions of tunnels where not a ray of sunlight enters and of hunger.
Step 1 (the Naturalist experiment): Based on notes from on-site reporting at the mine, it vividly records how wretched environment and hereditary impulses determine human behavior.

Step 2 (literary transcendence): But at the end of the novel, it presents a mythic, epic vision that, just as seeds sprout beneath the earth (germinal, the month of sprouting), the awakening of the workers will one day bloom into vast social transformation.
Interpretation: it shows the dynamic power of Zola's literature, which goes beyond the limits of mechanical determinism.

fl-15.title: The Poetics of French Symbolism (Symbolisme): Baudelaire, Verlaine, Rimbaud, and Mallarmé
explain: In the latter half of the 19th century, while prose literature moved toward the precise representation of external reality through Realism and Naturalism, poetry (Poésie) did the opposite: rejecting both the exaggerated outpouring of feeling of Romanticism and positivist description, it brought about the revolution of **Symbolism** (Symbolisme), which suggests the secrets of the invisible world. The starting point of this revolution in modern poetry is **Charles Baudelaire**'s (1821-1867) collection **Les Fleurs du mal**, published in 1857, in the same year as Flaubert's Madame Bovary, and which like it was tried for offending public morals.

Baudelaire drew eternal artistic **ideal** (Idéal) and beauty out of the everyday life of Paris, the ugly and diseased modern metropolis, and out of ennui and **spleen** (Spleen) ('beauty fished out of evil'). In particular, in the sonnet **"Correspondances"** (Correspondences) he called nature "a temple where living pillars sometimes let confused words escape," and sang that man walks through **"forests of symbols"** (forêts de symboles). Two kinds of correspondence occur here. One is **horizontal correspondence** (synesthesia: "perfumes, colors, and sounds answer one another"), in which the senses answer one another, and the other is **vertical correspondence**, in which sensory things are linked to the invisible spiritual and transcendent world. He also established the genre of the **prose poem** (Poème en prose) through *Le Spleen de Paris*, which sang of the crowds and solitude of Paris in prose.

The three poets who followed Baudelaire, **Paul Verlaine**, **Arthur Rimbaud**, and **Stéphane Mallarmé**, each pushed Symbolist poetics to a different extreme. In his "Art poétique" (*Art poétique*), Verlaine cried out **"Music before all else"** (*De la musique avant toute chose*), and in place of oratorical lessons or sharp colors made vague nuance and musical resonance the life of poetry.

**Rimbaud**, a genius poet who wrote like a flame and then gave up writing after only five years, from age fifteen to twenty, declared in the "Lettre du voyant" (*Lettre du voyant*, 1871) that **"the poet must make himself a seer (Voyant) through a long, immense, and reasoned derangement of all the senses."** Through the famous proposition that broke the modern myth of unity, **"I is another"** (*Je est un autre*), he unearthed an unknown world beyond the controlled conscious self, and with the prose-poem collections *Illuminations* and *Une saison en enfer* he opened the way to Surrealism.

**Mallarmé** was the intellectual summit of Symbolism. He defined it thus: **"To name an object is to do away with three quarters of the enjoyment of the poem, which is made of the happiness of guessing little by little; to suggest (Suggérer), that is the dream."** Mallarmé's experiment, rejecting the language of everyday communication and summoning an absent pure idea (absolute beauty) through the musical and syntactic arrangement of words, reached its extreme in his posthumous work *Un coup de dés jamais n'abolira le hasard*, in which the blank space of the page and the arrangement of the type are composed like a musical score.

examples.title: Analyzing the synesthesia and symbolic structure of Baudelaire's "Correspondances"
body: Condition: analyze the lines "There are perfumes fresh as the flesh of children, sweet as oboes, green as meadows."
Step 1: Smell (perfume) overlaps across boundaries with touch (flesh), hearing (the sound of oboes), and sight (green meadows) (horizontal correspondence, synesthesia).
Step 2: Through this fusion of senses, the poet becomes the one (the translator) who deciphers the fundamental, spiritual unity (vertical correspondence) beyond the fragmented material world.
Interpretation: where Realism observed the outer form of things, Symbolism read the invisible relations of correspondence behind things.

examples.title: The grammatical violation and poetic meaning of Rimbaud's 'Je est un autre'
body: Condition: in standard French grammar, the first person singular subject *Je* must be followed by *suis* (*Je suis*). But Rimbaud used the third person singular verb *est* and wrote *Je est un autre*.
Step 1: Through this deliberate grammatical violation, he shows that the thinking I (*Je*) operates like a third party (*est un autre*) that I cannot control.
Step 2: It overturns the rational, unified subject of 'I think, therefore I am,' which since Descartes had been a pillar of French philosophy.

Interpretation: it is a declaration that the poet is not someone who composes poems from his own consciousness but a channel (a seer) through which the voice of another resounds amid the derangement of the unconscious and the senses.

fl-16.title: Marcel Proust and In Search of Lost Time: Involuntary Memory and the Recovery of Time
explain: The great monument that opened the door of the 20th-century French novel is the seven-part epic novel **In Search of Lost Time** (À la recherche du temps perdu, 1913-1927), which **Marcel Proust** (1871-1922) wrote during the last fourteen years of his life, shut in a room soundproofed with cork. Where the 19th-century Balzacian novel arranged the events of external society in chronological order from an omniscient viewpoint, Proust made the **subjective consciousness, time, and the mechanism of memory** of the first-person narrator 'I' (Marcel) themselves the protagonist of the novel.

Proust strictly distinguishes two kinds of human memory. The first is **voluntary memory** (Mémoire volontaire), in which one deliberately tries to recall the past by means of the intellect (reason). The past that voluntary memory returns is as dry and fragmented as scraps of black-and-white photographs from which feeling and life have drained away, and it cannot revive the essence of the true past.

The second is **involuntary memory** (Mémoire involontaire), in which, through a sensory stimulus encountered by chance (taste, smell, touch, sound), the whole of past time suddenly comes back to life within a present sensation, regardless of our will. The most famous passage is the **episode of the madeleine dipped in tea** in the first volume, *Du côté de chez Swann*. One winter day, the moment he puts into his mouth a crumb of a little madeleine soaked in the tea his mother offered, the narrator is overwhelmed by an inexplicable, ecstatic joy. And in that taste and fragrance, together with the memory of the madeleine his Aunt Léonie used to give him in Combray in his childhood, the whole forgotten village of Combray, its house, garden, and people, comes back to life entire, as Japanese paper flowers unfold in water.

At the moment involuntary memory occurs in this way, the sensation of the past and the sensation of the present are superimposed into one, and the human being, escaping the violence of physical time that flows away and perishes, experiences **a pure essence beyond time** (timeless being). In the seventh and last volume of the novel, **Le Temps retrouvé** (Time Regained), the aged narrator experiences the miracle of involuntary memory in succession through the touch of stepping on uneven paving stones in the courtyard of the Guermantes mansion, the sound of a spoon striking a plate, and the feel of a stiff napkin.

At that moment the narrator realizes that all the 'lost time' he believed he had wasted in the vanity and jealousy of high society can in fact be **redeemed forever as 'time regained' through the creation of literature (art)**. And at the very moment of that realization, a great **circular structure** is completed: the book the narrator begins to write is none other than In Search of Lost Time itself, which the reader has been reading. Proust's characteristic **long-sentence style**, in which compound sentences, relative clauses, and metaphors branch out layer upon layer, was the inevitable form for holding in a single breath the many layers of time and the subtle undulations of psychology.

examples.title: Analyzing the sensory-medium structure of the madeleine episode
body: Condition: for a long time, whenever the narrator tried to recall childhood Combray with his mind, he could remember at most only the dry image of a corner of the staircase where he went up to bed in the evening (the limit of voluntary memory).
Step 1: By chance, in the present, he encounters a sensory impression identical to one from the past: 'the taste and aroma of a madeleine dipped in tea' (taste and smell).

Step 2: The sensory coincidence that bypassed the censorship of the intellect becomes the trigger, and the whole of the feeling and space of childhood, sealed deep in the unconscious, gushes up into the present (involuntary memory).
Interpretation: for Proust, truth lies not in abstract intellect but in the deep memory opened by a chance sensory encounter.

examples.title: The circular structure from Du côté de chez Swann to Le Temps retrouvé
body: Condition: the novel begins with the voice of a narrator in a half-asleep state before falling asleep, groping in the dark for the position of his body and for old rooms, passes through the disillusionment of high society and the painful love for Albertine, and ends in the last volume with the realization of his calling as an artist.
Step 1: Volumes 1 through 6 are the process of 'lost time', in which the narrator, in the flow of time, experiences the collapse of the illusions of love and of high society.

Step 2: In the last volume 7, Le Temps retrouvé, the narrator who has grasped the principle of involuntary memory finally decides to write the novel and returns to the first sentence of the first volume.
Interpretation: it is the summit of the modernist art-novel, holding that time lost in life is restored forever only through the form of art.

fl-17.title: Existentialism and the Literature of the Absurd: Sartre's Engagement and Camus's Revolt
explain: The Great Depression of the 1930s, the rise of fascism, and the experience of the Nazi German occupation and the Resistance in the Second World War shifted the central question of French literature from 'inner memory' to **'human freedom and responsibility before history.'** The two giants who led this era were **Jean-Paul Sartre** (1905-1980) and **Albert Camus** (1913-1960).

In his first novel, **La Nausée** (1938), Sartre portrayed the scene in which the protagonist Roquentin, gazing at the roots of a chestnut tree in a park, realizes that things simply exist there by chance, without any necessary reason or purpose (**contingency**, Contingence), and feels ontological vertigo and nausea. The core proposition of Sartrean existentialism is **"existence precedes essence"** (*L'existence précède l'essence*). Tools such as a knife or a watch are made after the maker has first conceived their purpose (essence), but the human being, thrown into a world without God, first exists and then **makes himself only through his own free choices and actions**. Therefore "man is condemned to be free" and must bear heavy responsibility for all his choices.

explain.alt: A table comparing the three peaks of 20th-century French narrative (Proust, the existentialists Sartre and Camus, and the nouveau roman) by core problem, core concepts, narrative technique, and representative works.
explain.caption: From the restoration of subjective time (Proust), through freedom and participation in history (existentialism), to the dismantling of the norms of the novel itself (the nouveau roman).

explain: The theory of literature that Sartre drew from this philosophy is the **engagement** (Engagement, social commitment) proclaimed in *Qu'est-ce que la littérature ?* (1947). He held that if poetry (Poésie) is the art that treats language as a thing, prose (Prose) is the art that uses language as an instrument of action to reveal and change the world. Therefore he insisted that the prose writer cannot remain silent or stand by, but must write **engaged literature** (Littérature engagée), defending freedom against the injustices of his own time.

Meanwhile the Algerian-born writer **Albert Camus** established the literature of the **absurd** (Absurde) in 1942 with the novel **L'Étranger** (The Stranger) and the philosophical essay **Le Mythe de Sisyphe** (The Myth of Sisyphus). The absurd arises not merely because the world itself is irrational, but from the **confrontation (collision) between the human cry for meaning and unity and a world that finally refuses rational meaning with silence**. In L'Étranger, the protagonist Meursault is tried over the incident in which, because he did not weep at his mother's funeral and because of the glare of the sun, he shot an Arab, and he is sentenced to death less for the act of killing itself than for not having acted out false feelings in keeping with social convention and the theater of morality. Roland Barthes called the dry short-sentence style of L'Étranger in the **passé composé**, stripped of causal explanation and rhetorical ornament, **"the zero degree of writing"** (Degré zéro de l'écriture, white writing).

Camus then, through the figure of Sisyphus pushing up again the rock that endlessly rolls down from the mountaintop, presented not resignation or suicide but **revolt** (Révolte), a direct gaze at the absurd, and through the novel **La Peste** (1947), in which Dr. Rieux and the citizens of the closed city of Oran silently fight against suffering as a plague sweeps through, he moved on to **human solidarity** beyond the individual absurd (*"I revolt, therefore we are"*).

examples.title: Analyzing Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' and bad faith (Mauvaise foi)
body: Condition: there is a waiter who acts mechanically as if he had been determined from birth, for ever, to be 'a thing called a waiter', or conversely a person who blames his past failures on his 'unavoidable innate character'.
Step 1: According to Sartre, a human being has no fixed essence (destiny or nature) decided in advance.

Step 2: The attitude of deceiving oneself into pretending to be a thing or the product of unavoidable circumstances, in order to flee the anxiety of being a free subject, Sartre criticized as **bad faith** (Mauvaise foi).
Interpretation: literature is a summons that makes the reader break this bad faith and face freedom and responsibility.

examples.title: The formal correspondence between the 'passé composé' style of Camus's L'Étranger and the absurd
body: Condition: the whole of Part One of L'Étranger, beginning with its first sentence *Aujourd'hui, maman est morte. Ou peut-être hier, je ne sais pas.* (Today, Maman died. Or maybe yesterday, I don't know), is written with nearly every sentence as a short **passé composé** sentence.

Step 1: Where the traditional novel used the imparfait and subordinate clauses to join the causal relations and psychology among events smoothly, the passé composé sentences of L'Étranger break off like a 'string of isolated presents', fragmented without causal links to one another.
Step 2: In his commentary on L'Étranger, Sartre analyzed this passé composé sentence as the very style that embodies, in itself, an 'absurd world and time' in which the links of meaning are cut.

Interpretation: it is a representative case in which the syntactic feature of the passé composé learned in stage 2 (punctual, discontinuous perfective aspect) is sublimated into a literary technique for expressing philosophical absurdity.

fl-18.title: The Nouveau Roman and the Theater of the Absurd to Contemporary French Literature
explain: In the mid-1950s, an avant-garde movement of experimental fiction arose in the French literary world that rose up head-on not only against the norms of the traditional novel since Balzac but also against Sartrean engaged literature (using the novel as a vehicle for political and philosophical messages). It was the **Nouveau Roman** (the New Novel) of writers gathered around the publishing house Éditions de Minuit. The principal writers were **Alain Robbe-Grillet**, **Nathalie Sarraute**, **Michel Butor**, and **Claude Simon**, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Nathalie Sarraute, in her essay collection **L'Ère du soupçon** (1956), declared that readers and writers today no longer believe in the 'plausible characters' that the traditional novel puts forward. Robbe-Grillet likewise, in **Pour un nouveau roman** (1963), argued that the four outworn myths that had supported the traditional novel must all be discarded: **(1) the character (Personnage) with a distinct name and personality, (2) the plot (Histoire) with a beginning, development, turn, and conclusion, (3) political and moral commitment (Engagement), and (4) the dichotomy of form and content**.

What, instead, did the nouveau roman show? Robbe-Grillet rejected personifying metaphors that project human feelings onto things (for example, "capricious weather," "sad landscape") and presented **chosisme (thing-ism, a literature of the gaze)**, which records only the position, size, and geometrical angles of things as coldly and minutely as a camera lens. In his novel **La Jalousie** (1957), the title *jalousie* carries the double meaning of the husband's 'jealousy' and the 'slats of a blind' on a house in a tropical colony. The narrator 'I' (*Je*), the husband, never appears even once in the novel; only the movements of his wife A..., seen through the gaps of the blind, the glass on the table, and the trace of a centipede crushed on the wall are described repeatedly with their chronological order scrambled, reproducing the gaze of an obsessive consciousness itself.

On the stage of the same 1950s, the **theater of the absurd** (Théâtre de l'absurde), led by Samuel **Beckett**'s **En attendant Godot** (1953) and Eugène **Ionesco**'s **La Cantatrice chauve**, burst forth. If Camus and Sartre still tried to explain the theme of the absurd with logical dialogue and plot, Beckett and Ionesco **dismantled plot, causality, and the communicative function of language itself on the stage**. In En attendant Godot, the two tramps Vladimir and Estragon fill time with meaningless conversation and wordplay while waiting for a 'Godot' who never comes, and through this they showed the fundamental emptiness and waiting of human existence in the form of the stage itself.

French literature, decentered through structuralist and post-structuralist criticism of the late 1960s (Roland Barthes's "The Death of the Author," Foucault, Derrida), met from the 1980s onward **the return of story and the subject**. **Marguerite Duras** (*L'Amant*) portrayed love and desire in a style of silence and restraint; **Patrick Modiano**, a Nobel laureate (*Rue des boutiques obscures*), explored the foggy memory of occupied Paris and the tracing of identity; and **Annie Ernaux** (*Les Années*, Nobel Prize in Literature 2022) opened a new horizon of contemporary literature with a 'transpersonal autobiography' that sociologically combines the intimate experience of the individual with the collective memory of an era, and with a knife-edge plain style (écriture plate).

examples.title: The double title and the absent narrator of Robbe-Grillet's La Jalousie
body: Condition: the novel La Jalousie has not a single line of psychological narration such as "I feel jealous because it seems my wife is having an affair with my friend Franck." Instead, only the angle of the shadows of the terrace railing, the hand movements of the wife and the position of Franck seen through the slats of the blind (jalousie), and the number of ice glasses on the table are described obsessively.
Step 1: It completely abandons the technique of the 19th-century traditional novel in which the narrator directly explains a character's inner psychology.

Step 2: Instead, the geometrical landscape description itself, in which the gaze of an invisible observer with neither a name nor a pronoun (*Je*) measures and replays things, constitutes the state of burning 'jealous' consciousness.
Interpretation: it is the essence of the nouveau roman, in which an extremely objective gaze at external things paradoxically reveals the most extreme subjective obsession.

examples.title: The experiment with second-person plural 'Vous' narration in Michel Butor's La Modification
body: Condition: the novel La Modification (1957), which deals with the change in consciousness of a man on a train from Paris to Rome until he gives up his original resolve to go to his mistress and decides to return to his wife, addresses the protagonist from beginning to end in the **second person 'you' (Vous)** (*Vous avez mis votre pied gauche...*).
Step 1: It introduces narration in the **second person (Vous)**, which is neither the subjective confession of the first person (*Je*) nor the omniscient observation of the third person (*Il*).

Step 2: The reader is directly summoned into the seat of the protagonist sitting in the train compartment, and goes through with him, in real time, the process in which his consciousness wavers and transforms.
Interpretation: it shows that the nouveau roman was not mere destruction but a refined formal experiment for a new reading experience and an exploration of consciousness.

fl-19.title: Bachelor's Capstone I: Deciphering Complex Constructions of French Tense, Mood, and Pronouns, and Identifying Literary-Historical Movements
explain: In the first lesson of the bachelor's capstone, we combine the **French syntactic and grammatical system** learned in stage 2 (the aspectual contrast of the passé composé, imparfait, and plus-que-parfait and past participle agreement, the choice between subjunctive and indicative, the conditional and si-clauses, and double pronoun order) with the **movements in the history of French literature** learned in stages 3 to 5 (from 17th-century classicism to the 20th-century nouveau roman), and decipher original sentences and critical texts across both.

The **three-step syntactic analysis protocol** for precisely deciphering sentences from French originals is as follows. In **step 1 (identifying tense, mood, and clause structure)**, first determine the tense of the main-clause verb and the subordinate-clause verb (imparfait background versus passé composé event, plus-que-parfait prior event) and the mood (indicative factual statement, subjunctive subjective attitude or concession, conditional supposition, future in the past, and free indirect discourse). In **step 2 (tracing antecedent pronouns and past-participle gender and number agreement)**, find the antecedent noun to which the object pronoun (*le, la, les, lui, leur, y, en*) or relative pronoun (*que*) placed before the verb refers, and verify the grammatical agreement through whether the past participle ending (*-e, -s, -es*) agrees. In **step 3 (reading discourse and stylistic effect)**, interpret what narrative distance and viewpoint the construction creates.

For example, let us decipher the following sentence: *Bien qu'elle eût lu les lettres qu'il lui avait envoyées, elle a agi comme si rien ne s'était passé.* (Although she had read the letters he had sent her, she acted as if nothing had happened.) In the first clause, the pluperfect subjunctive (*eût lu*) is used after the concessive conjunction *Bien que*; in the relative clause *qu'il lui avait envoyées*, the direct-object relative pronoun *que (qu')*, standing for the feminine plural antecedent *les lettres*, comes before the pluperfect verb, so the *-es* agreement occurs on the past participle *envoyées*, and the indirect-object pronoun *lui* is placed before the auxiliary.

On top of syntactic deciphering, identify the **aesthetic markers of each era** in the text. If duty and passion clash within twelve-syllable alexandrine verse, the rule of the three unities, and the norm of propriety, it is **17th-century classical tragedy** (Corneille, Racine); if intolerance is satirized through a foreigner's letters or a philosophical tale, it is **18th-century Enlightenment** (Montesquieu, Voltaire).

If it depicts the human types of capitalism through description of a boardinghouse environment and reappearing characters, it is **Balzac's realism**; if it uses third-person imperfect free indirect discourse and non-intervening objectivity, **Flaubert**; if it sets out an experimental novel of heredity and environment, **Zola's Naturalism**; if it pursues synesthetic correspondence and suggestion, **Symbolist poetics** (Baudelaire, Rimbaud, Mallarmé); if it follows involuntary memory awakened by the senses in a long periodic style, **Proust**; if it presents a dry passé composé zero-degree style with the absurd and engagement, **existentialist and absurdist literature** (Sartre, Camus); and if it erases character and plot and describes only the geometrical exterior of things, the **nouveau roman** (Robbe-Grillet).

examples.title: Integrated deciphering of tense, pronoun, and agreement in a complex grammatical sentence
body: Condition: the sentence *Si elle avait retrouvé cette saveur autrefois, elle s'en serait souvenue toute sa vie.* (If she had found that taste again long ago, she would have remembered it all her life.)
Step 1 (conditional structure): it is a **supposition contrary to a past fact** made of *Si + pluperfect (avait retrouvé)* and a main clause in the *past conditional (se serait souvenue)*.

Step 2 (pronoun and agreement): in the pronominal verb *se souvenir de* (to remember), *de cette saveur* is replaced by the neuter pronoun **en** and placed between the reflexive pronoun *s'* and the auxiliary *serait* (*s'en serait*), and since it is a pronominal verb taking the auxiliary *être*, the past participle *souvenue* agrees with the subject *elle* in the feminine singular.
Interpretation: through grammatical analysis we can read exactly the supposition of a sensory memory that did not occur in the past.

examples.title: The stylistic contrast in literary history created by the choice of tense (imparfait vs passé composé)
body: Condition: Text A combines the third-person imparfait (Imparfait) with exclamatory sentences to show the romantic daydreams of a provincial doctor's wife without any intervention by the narrator. Text B strings together short first-person passé composé (Passé composé) sentences without causal conjunctions and dryly reports a mother's funeral and a murder on the beach.
Step 1: Text A shows **free indirect discourse** using the imparfait and **non-intervening objectivity**, so it is Flaubert's Madame Bovary of the 19th century.
Step 2: Text B shows the **zero degree of writing (white writing)** through a discontinuous passé composé and the **absurd** of the world, so it is Camus's L'Étranger of the 20th century.
Interpretation: the tenses of French grammar (imparfait versus passé composé) operate as the decisive stylistic device that divides movements in literary history.

fl-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone II: French Text Stylistic Analysis and Designing a Literary Criticism Essay
explain: The final capstone task of the French language and literature bachelor's program is to integrate the tools of French grammatical and stylistic analysis with the theories of literary-historical criticism and write a single complete critical essay. In the French literary tradition, since Lanson, the discipline known as **explication de texte** (Explication de texte) has been wary of discussing only the broad ideas of a work in the abstract, and has made central the training of demonstrating **how philosophical and aesthetic meaning is born from the micro-level forms of a sentence's tense, mood, vocabulary, and syntax**.

A model French-literature critical essay is composed in the following four steps. **(1) Posing the problem (Problématique) and setting the object of analysis**: choose the literary movements or writers to be analyzed (for example, classical tragedy versus Romanticism, Realism and Naturalism versus Symbolism, Proust's novel of memory versus existentialism and the nouveau roman) and present the central question. **(2) Analyzing French syntactic and stylistic devices**: analyze the linguistic evidence at work in the text, such as tense and aspect (the duration and background of the imparfait and free indirect discourse versus the discontinuous events and zero-degree style of the passé composé), mood (the subjective inflection of the subjunctive, the supposition and distancing of the conditional), and sentence breath (Proust's periodic compound sentences versus Camus's short sentences).

**(3) Comparative argument in literary history and aesthetics**: argue, contrasting at least two movements, how the stylistic features analyzed above embody the aesthetic principles of their time (the three unities and propriety, practical enlightenment and satire, non-intervening objectivity and the experimental novel, universal correspondence and suggestion, involuntary memory, existential engagement and the absurd, the nouveau roman's description of things). **(4) Critical synthesis and reflection on limits**: close by summarizing how later movements overcame or varied the limits left by earlier ones.

After finishing the writing, use the checklist to examine for yourself whether the concepts of French grammar and the concepts of literary history are not merely listed superficially but closely interlocked in a single argument.

examples.title: A sample critical paragraph combining French tense (imparfait vs passé composé) and the aesthetics of the novel
body: Topic: comparing the aesthetic role played by the past tenses in the realism of Flaubert in the 19th century and the absurd novel of Camus in the 20th century.

Step 1 (linguistic and stylistic analysis): The French imparfait (Imparfait) is an imperfective tense expressing boundless duration and states, and the passé composé (Passé composé) is a tense expressing a completed, punctual event.

Step 2 (combining literary criticism): In Madame Bovary, Flaubert employed 'free indirect discourse' built on the imparfait, so that without the narrator's direct intervention the reader is kept within the protagonist's endless boredom and romantic illusion. Conversely, in L'Étranger, Camus, by chaining short 'passé composé' sentences that exclude causal conjunctions, embodied in grammatical form itself a worldview of the 'absurd' in which events flow by chopped up, without any necessary link of meaning.

Interpretation: in this way the difference in grammatical tense and aspect becomes the aesthetic watershed dividing the psychological and realist representation of the 19th century from the existential absurd of the 20th.
